Entry into a Material Definitive Agreement.
Upsized Revolving Credit Facility
On November 23, 2026, DoorDash, Inc., a Nevada corporation (the “Company”),
 entered into a Commitment Increase Supplement (the “Commitment Increase Supplement”) to its existing Revolving Credit and Guaranty Agreement, dated as of November 19, 2019 (as
 previously amended and restated as of August 5, 2026, the “Existing RCF Credit Agreement” and, as amended by the Commitment Increase Supplement, the “RCF Credit Agreement”), in each case, among the Company, as the borrower, the guarantors party thereto from time to time (if any), the lenders and issuing banks party thereto from time to time and
 JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., as administrative agent, providing for, among other things, a senior unsecured revolving credit facility (the “RCF Facility”) that matures on August
 5, 2031. The Commitment Increase Supplement, among other things, increased the total revolving commitments under the Existing RCF Credit Agreement by $1.5 billion, from a total of $2.0 billion
 to a total of $3.5 billion. The amounts available under the RCF Credit Agreement are available to the Company to use for working capital and general corporate purposes, including for certain permitted stock repurchases and acquisitions. The terms
 of the RCF Credit Agreement and the RCF Facility remain otherwise unchanged.
Term Loan Credit Facility
In connection with the pending acquisition (the “Acquisition”) by the Company of Maplebear Inc.
 d.b.a. Instacart, a Delaware corporation (“Instacart”), pursuant to a contemplated merger of Ibiza Merger Sub, Inc., a Delaware corporation and a wholly owned subsidiary of the
 Company (“Merger Sub”), with and into Instacart, with Instacart surviving as a subsidiary of the Company, pursuant to the terms and subject to the conditions set forth in the
 Agreement and Plan of Merger, dated as of October 28, 2026 (as amended, restated, amended and restated, supplemented or otherwise modified from time to time, the “Merger Agreement”),
 among the Company, Merger Sub and Instacart, which was previously disclosed in a Current Report on Form 8-K filed by the Company with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC”)
 on October 29, 2026 (the “Signing Form 8-K”), the Company, on November 23, 2026, entered into a senior unsecured delayed draw term loan credit facility in an aggregate
 principal amount of $1.792 billion (the “Term Loan Facility”), pursuant to a Term Loan Credit and Guaranty Agreement (the “Term Loan Credit Agreement”), among the Company, as the borrower, the guarantors from time to time party thereto (if any), the lenders from time to time party thereto and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., as administrative
 agent (the “TL Agent”). The Term Loan Credit Agreement permits the Company to increase the aggregate amount of commitments under the Term Loan Credit Agreement on or prior to
 the funding date under the Term Loan Credit Agreement, so long as the aggregate amount of such increase does not cause the aggregate commitments to exceed $2.0 billion, subject to the receipt of additional commitments from existing and/or new
 lenders and other conditions to be agreed.
Subject to the limited conditionality provisions set forth in the Term Loan Credit Agreement, the loans under the Term Loan Credit Agreement are available to be drawn
 in a single draw until the earliest of (i) five business days after the Outside Date (as defined in the Merger Agreement, subject to certain extensions and limitations set forth in the Term Loan Credit Agreement), (ii) the valid termination of the
 Merger Agreement in accordance with its terms, (iii) the closing of the Acquisition without funding the loans under the Term Loan Credit Agreement, and (iv) receipt by the TL Agent of written notice from the Company of its election to terminate the
 commitments under the Term Loan Credit Agreement. The proceeds of the loans to be extended under the Term Loan Facility are expected to be used to finance, among other
 things, the consummation of the Acquisition, the refinancing of certain debt of Instacart and the payment of fees, costs and expenses related to the foregoing. The Term Loan Facility will have no required amortization and will mature on the third
 anniversary after the funding date thereunder. Loans under the Term Loan Facility that are repaid or prepaid may not be reborrowed.
Loans under the Term Loan Facility will bear interest, at the Company’s option, at (i) a base rate equal to the highest of (A) the prime rate, (B) the higher of the
 federal funds effective rate or a composite overnight bank borrowing rate plus 0.50%, and (C) Term Secured Overnight Financing Rate (“Term SOFR”) for a one-month interest
 period plus 1.00% or (ii) Term SOFR (based on an interest period of one, three or six months), in each case, plus an initial margin of 1.00%, subject to potential step-downs to 0.875% or 0.750% based on certain of the Company’s credit ratings as
 specified in the Term Loan Credit Agreement (the “Company’s Applicable Rating”). The Company is also obligated to pay other customary fees for a credit facility of this size
 and type, including an arrangement fee, administration fees and a ticking fee. Such ticking fee will accrue, beginning on February 25, 2027, on the daily aggregate amount of unfunded delayed draw term loan commitments at a rate ranging from 0.08%
 to 0.10% per annum, based on the Company’s Applicable Rating. The Company will have the right to prepay the outstanding loans under the Term Loan Facility, in whole or in part, without premium or penalty.
The Company’s obligations under the Term Loan Facility are not secured and are not currently guaranteed by any of its subsidiaries. The Term Loan Credit Agreement
 contains representations and warranties, affirmative and negative covenants and events of default provisions that are substantially similar to those in the RCF Credit Agreement, subject to
 customary “certain funds” and limited conditionality provisions governing funding at the closing of the Acquisition.
The foregoing summaries of the Commitment Increase Supplement and the Term Loan Credit Agreement are not complete and are qualified in their entirety by reference to
 the full text of the Existing RCF Credit Agreement, as supplemented by the Commitment Increase Supplement, and the Term Loan Credit Agreement, as applicable. Copies of the Commitment Increase Supplement and the Term Loan Credit Agreement are
 attached as Exhibit 10.1 and 10.2, respectively, to this Current Report on Form 8-K and are incorporated by reference in their entirety.

CrowdStrike to
Acquire Zscaler, Bringing Network Security and Zero Trust to the Falcon Platform
 | | ● | Acquisition will unite the leaders
 in securing every device and every connection
 | | ● | Zscaler will expand CrowdStrike’s
 total addressable market by more than $185 billion
 | | ● | Will provide a path to cross-sell
 the CrowdStrike platform to approximately 8,000 Zscaler customers
 | | ● | Will deliver Zero Trust for AI
 Safety, securing the last mile of agentic AI
 | | ● | Combined company is expected to
 begin with more than $10 billion in combined annual recurring revenue
AUSTIN, Texas and SANTA CLARA, Calif.
– November 23, 2026 – CrowdStrike (NASDAQ: CRWD) and Zscaler (NASDAQ: ZS) today announced that they have
entered into a definitive agreement under which CrowdStrike will acquire Zscaler in an all-stock transaction that values Zscaler at approximately
$43.9 billion. Under the terms of the agreement, Zscaler shareholders will receive 1.135 shares of CrowdStrike common stock for each
share of Zscaler common stock they own.
Network Security on the CrowdStrike
Falcon Platform
With Zscaler, CrowdStrike will enter
network security, cybersecurity’s largest single addressable market segment. Users, applications, and now AI agents connect directly
to the cloud, and that traffic never comes back through the data center. Firewalls and VPNs built to guard the data center can’t
see, inspect, or stop that traffic, the threats coming in, or the data going out. Zscaler’s SSE is purpose-built for the AI era,
with the Zscaler Zero Trust Exchange sitting inline between every user, agent, and application to enforce zero trust on every connection.
SASE builds on that foundation to bring security and the network together, creating zero trust everywhere.
CrowdStrike is a leader in securing
the endpoint, the workload, the identity, and the data. Zscaler is a leader in securing the connections between them. After closing,
CrowdStrike will unite endpoint security with Zero Trust SASE to deliver a unified platform that puts both controls in the adversary’s
path to stop breaches.
“Security used to be about keeping
the adversary out. Today, safety is required to let AI in,” said George Kurtz, CEO and founder of CrowdStrike. “The network
used to connect people to places. Now it connects agents to data. With Zscaler, we’re building cybersecurity’s operating
system: a single control plane to deploy AI, control AI, and enable any agentic application to run safely. We see a path to become the
largest AI safety and security company the world has ever seen.”
“We built Zscaler to bring a new
approach to the cybersecurity industry and that is a Zero Trust architecture,” said Jay Chaudhry, CEO, chairman, and founder of
Zscaler. “In the AI era, Zero Trust security has become non-negotiable, and AI agents are rapidly becoming the new weakest link.
This agreement will accelerate our ability to bring Zero Trust Everywhere to a larger customer base. We see a significant opportunity
to offer customers far superior protection in a rapidly evolving threat landscape and enable enterprises to safely adopt AI. Zscaler
and CrowdStrike are complementary and this is the natural evolution of our longstanding partnership. We look forward to enabling our
employees, customers, and shareholders to be a part of the significant upside that this transaction brings.”
One Platform, One Data Layer, One
Flex Contract
With Zscaler, the Falcon platform will
own the two most important control points: the Falcon sensor across every endpoint and cloud workload, and the Zero Trust Exchange on
every user, agent, and application connection. The endpoint is where the agent runs. The network is where it goes. Falcon Next-Gen SIEM,
the agentic SOC, will unify device and network telemetry into one security data set. Falcon Flex will bring Zscaler onto the commercial
model customers already use, so they commit once and expand from there.
Strategic Rationale and Value Creation
Opportunity
 | | ● | Brings Zscaler’s Zero
 Trust SASE, Security for AI, and Data Protection to the Falcon Platform: Zscaler protects
 50 percent of the Fortune 500 and operates the world’s largest distributed inline security
 cloud across more than 200 service locations. After closing, CrowdStrike will offer Zscaler’s
 Zero Trust SASE, security for AI, and data protection as part of the Falcon platform.
 | | ● | Combines Device and Network
 Data: The Falcon platform generates trillions of events daily from the endpoint and cloud
 workloads, and Zscaler’s Zero Trust Exchange processes more than 750 billion transactions
 per day. After closing, device and network telemetry will converge into a single data set,
 allowing CrowdStrike’s SafeMind frontier security models to train on the adversary’s
 full attack path.
 | | ● | Unlocks Cross-Sell Across Both
 Customer Bases: Approximately 8,000 Zscaler customers are not yet CrowdStrike customers.
 Within the shared customer base, CrowdStrike sees room for even more platform adoption. After
 closing, customers of either company will be able to add the other’s products on a
 single Falcon Flex contract. Both companies have best-in-class gross and net retention.
 | | ● | Expands the Market and the
 Partner Ecosystem: CrowdStrike estimates the acquisition will expand its total addressable
 market by more than $185 billion in calendar year 2029. Zscaler’s solutions will be
 sold through CrowdStrike’s global system integrators, resellers, distributors, and
 cloud marketplaces, with significant opportunity downmarket and into the MSSP space.
 | | ● | From Partnership to One Platform:
 The acquisition builds on one of CrowdStrike’s largest technology alliances, spanning
 more than 2,000 shared customers and 16 integrations. For years, customers have asked CrowdStrike
 and Zscaler to join forces, and the two companies come together from positions of strength.
 A partnership integrates separate products. One company integrates everything: the data,
 the roadmap, the go-to-market, and the commercial model, and AI accelerates the integration.
 After closing, the integration of Zscaler into the Falcon platform will give customers one
 platform, one data layer, and one contract.
 | | ● | Increases Scale and Accelerates
 Profitable Growth: At closing, the combined company is expected to begin with more than
 $10 billion in ARR. Zscaler reported $3.9 billion of ARR as of its recently completed fiscal
 quarter. The acquisition is expected to add incremental high-margin recurring revenue streams
 to CrowdStrike’s financial profile.
 | | ● | Creates Significant Revenue
 Synergies: CrowdStrike expects revenue synergies to build progressively over the first
 30 months following close, reaching approximately $1 billion in annualized run-rate revenue
 synergies by the end of that period. These revenue synergies are expected to come from deepening
 combined customer relationships, expanding cross-sell and upsell opportunities, and integrating
 Zscaler’s solutions into CrowdStrike’s Falcon Flex go-to-market motion.
 | | ● | Drives Margin Expansion and
 Free Cash Flow Accretion: CrowdStrike expects to achieve $500 million in annualized run-rate
 cost synergies within 18 to 24 months following the close, primarily through optimization
 of its data center infrastructure, vendors, and broader operations. These initiatives will
 support additional operating leverage and margin expansion over time. The transaction is
 expected to be significantly and immediately accretive to free cash flow per share before
 factoring in any synergies. The transaction is also expected to be accretive to revenue growth,
 non-GAAP operating margin, and free cash flow margin, after synergies, within the first fiscal
 year after close.
Transaction Details 
Under the terms of the agreement, which
has been unanimously approved by the boards of directors of both companies, CrowdStrike will acquire Zscaler in an all-stock transaction
valued at an enterprise value of approximately $43.9 billion, based on CrowdStrike’s closing share price as of November 20, 2026.
Each outstanding share of Zscaler common stock will be exchanged for 1.135 shares of CrowdStrike common stock, representing an implied
value of approximately $260.41 per Zscaler share, based on CrowdStrike’s closing share price as of November 20, 2026. This represents
a premium of approximately 34% to Zscaler’s closing share price as of November 20, 2026. Following completion of the transaction,
existing CrowdStrike shareholders are expected to own approximately 84.1% of the combined company, and existing Zscaler shareholders
approximately 15.9%.
The transaction is expected to close
in the second half of CrowdStrike’s fiscal year 2028, subject to approval by Zscaler shareholders, receipt of required regulatory
approvals, and satisfaction of other customary closing conditions. In connection with the transaction, Jay Chaudhry and his affiliates,
representing approximately 34% of Zscaler outstanding shares, have entered into voting agreements in support of the transaction. Until
closing, both companies will continue to operate independently.
Following the close of the transaction,
Jay Chaudhry will continue to lead the Zscaler business and will join the CrowdStrike Board of Directors.
CrowdStrike Reports Fiscal Third
Quarter 2027 Results and Zscaler Issues Fiscal First Quarter 2027 Results
In a separate press release issued today,
CrowdStrike reported its fiscal third quarter 2027 financial results. CrowdStrike’s financial results are available on the Investor
Relations website at ir.crowdstrike.com.
CrowdStrike and Zscaler will hold a
joint conference call today, November 23, 2026, at 5:00 a.m. Pacific time (8:00 a.m. Eastern time) to discuss the transaction and CrowdStrike’s
fiscal third quarter 2027 financial results, replacing the call previously scheduled for December 1, 2026. An investor presentation regarding
the transaction will be available on CrowdStrike’s Investor Relations website at ir.crowdstrike.com. A recorded webcast of the
event will also be available there for one year.
Zscaler separately reported financial
results today for its fiscal first quarter 2027. Zscaler’s earnings release can be found at ir.zscaler.com.
Advisors 
Qatalyst Partners is serving as sole
lead financial advisor to CrowdStrike. J.P. Morgan Securities LLC and BofA Securities also advised CrowdStrike. Davis Polk & Wardwell
LLP is serving as legal counsel and Joele Frank is serving as strategic communications advisor.
BDT & MSD Partners is sole lead financial
advisor to Zscaler. Citigroup Global Markets Inc. and Goldman Sachs & Co. LLC are also named as financial advisors to Zscaler. Wilson
Sonsini Goodrich & Rosati LLP is serving as legal counsel and Kekst CNC is serving as strategic communications advisor.
About CrowdStrike 
CrowdStrike (NASDAQ: CRWD), a
global cybersecurity leader, has redefined modern security with the world’s most advanced cloud-native platform for protecting
critical areas of enterprise risk: endpoints and cloud workloads, identity, and data.
Powered by the CrowdStrike Security
Cloud and world-class AI, the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform leverages real-time indicators of attack, threat intelligence, evolving
adversary tradecraft, and enriched telemetry from across the enterprise to deliver hyper-accurate detections, automated protection and
remediation, elite threat hunting, and prioritized observability of vulnerabilities.
Purpose-built in the cloud with a single

complexity, and immediate time-to-value.

CrowdStrike Reports Third Quarter Fiscal Year 2027 Financial Results
•Announces definitive agreement to acquire Zscaler
•Delivers all-time record net new ARR of $419 million, accelerates growth to 58% year-over-year
•Ending ARR reaches $6.26 billion, accelerates growth for the fifth consecutive quarter to 27% year-over-year
•Increases FY27 net new ARR growth guidance by 1,060 basis points to 45% year-over-year growth at the midpoint
•Achieves all-time record cash flow from operations of $665 million and all-time record free cash flow of $474 million
AUSTIN, Texas, November 23, 2026 -- CrowdStrike Holdings, Inc. (Nasdaq: CRWD), today announced financial results for the third quarter fiscal year 2027, ended October 31, 2026.
“Q3 was the best quarter in CrowdStrike’s history,” said George Kurtz, CrowdStrike’s Founder and Chief Executive Officer. “Growth accelerated across the business as customers consolidated on the Falcon platform through Falcon Flex. Falcon Guardian, which secures AI agents across the enterprise, crossed $100 million in ARR in its first year following the quarter end. With today’s announced acquisition of Zscaler, we will add the network, entering security’s largest TAM as a scaled leader. Falcon is the security operating system for the agentic era.”
Burt Podbere, CrowdStrike's Chief Financial Officer, added, "Our Q3 results delivered record performance across the board, highlighted by all-time record net new ARR, cash flow from operations, free cash flow, and our all-time record pipeline entering Q4. Our strong business momentum gives us the confidence to significantly raise our full-year outlook. PRESS RELEASE
ECB expands acceptance of DLT-based assets as eligible Eurosystem collateral
23 November 2026
Eurosystem to accept assets issued on distributed ledger technology (DLT) platforms licensed under the EU DLT Pilot Regime Regulation and made available on the TARGET2-Securities platform as eligible collateral for Eurosystem credit operations
Decision is part of a roadmap to explore eligibility and on-chain mobilisation of assets issued and settled entirely on DLT networks
New milestone underlines Eurosystem’s commitment to innovation and fostering technological progress in European financial markets
The Governing Council of the European Central Bank (ECB) has approved the acceptance of marketable assets issued on DLT platforms licensed under the EU DLT Pilot Regime Regulation as eligible collateral for Eurosystem credit operations, subject to specific Eurosystem requirements. This is a new milestone in the roadmap towards making the Eurosystem collateral framework fit for a tokenised European financial market ecosystem, which entails exploring ways to accept and mobilise tokenised assets in their native form.
“We support innovation without lowering our standards”, says Executive Board member Isabel Schnabel. “A future-proof collateral framework must embrace new technologies without compromising on safety or the rigour of our risk assessment.”
The decision supports the expansion of the eligibility of DLT-based assets in the Eurosystem’s collateral framework through a measured, controlled and technology-neutral approach. At the same time, it ensures that the Eurosystem’s collateral framework remains robust, adaptable, future-proof and aligned with the Eurosystem’s broader work on tokenisation and Appia objectives.
To be eligible, the assets must meet all standard collateral eligibility criteria. The arrangements for mobilising these assets must comply with applicable Eurosystem requirements. This includes making the assets available to the Eurosystem via an eligible link to a central securities depository (CSD) operating an eligible securities settlement system. In line with the existing eligibility framework for Eurosystem credit operations, the securities settlement systems must comply with the Central Securities Depositories Regulation and offer settlement in the TARGET2-Securities platform. In addition to being licensed under the DLT Pilot Regime Regulation, DLT platforms will need to meet dedicated Eurosystem requirements to ensure legal certainty and operational safety regarding, for example, settlement finality designation and the outsourcing of critical functions. The Eurosystem expects to communicate the details of these requirements in the spring of 2027, with implementation planned to take effect in June 2027. 
As stated by ECB Executive Board member Piero Cipollone, “Pontes and Appia are helping turn Europe’s vision for tokenised finance into reality. And by adapting our collateral framework, we are further enabling the European tokenised finance market to grow, while upholding the principles of safety, efficiency and a level playing field.”
Today’s decision follows the announcement on 27 January 2026 to accept as collateral assets issued in CSDs using DLT-based services. While the Eurosystem’s roadmap foresees further exploration of ways to expand eligibility to assets issued and settled entirely on DLT networks, today’s decision will significantly contribute to the interoperability between DLT platforms and traditional systems, thereby fostering integration in the current hybrid environment.

General insurance stress test highlights value of rehearsing crisis response and recovery 
 The Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) has today published the results of its 2026 Dynamic General Insurance Stress Test (DyGIST) 
 Published on 
 23 November 2026 
News release
The DyGIST 2026 scenario consisted of a sequence of severe yet plausible insurance events unfolding over a three-week period (May 2026), including some significant natural catastrophes and cyber events, coupled with a financial market stress. The exercise involved 25 major insurers, representing more than 80% of the UK general insurance market. 
The severe combined scenario was designed to push most participating insurers beyond their internal risk appetite limits, to identify the actions they would take in response. Those actions included use of wider-group resources, including capital injections, credit facilities, dividend retention, alongside significant reliance on reinsurance. This provided insight into the importance of firms being confident that these actions would be available, timely and deliverable in a real market-wide stress. 
Insurers were also asked to treat the exercise as a test of their crisis management frameworks, including how they would assess emerging losses and respond in practice to the unfolding events. Those who did so most comprehensively identified the greatest opportunities to strengthen their arrangements, and have made changes to reflect lessons learned from the exercise. Effective responses mobilised relevant functions early, established clear ownership and escalation, made uncertainty visible through evolving estimates and assumptions, and showed how new information and challenge changed decisions. The exercise highlighted the benefit of testing the practical operation of crisis and recovery plans, rather than focusing only on financial impacts.
Reinsurance played an important role in the sector’s resilience in the scenario, reducing gross losses from the insurance events by around 72%. Reinsurance arrangements were well-diversified at a sector level. However, the exercise also highlighted the importance of firms understanding potential concentrations and dependencies within their own arrangements, particularly where resources may be shared across groups or relied upon by multiple firms during a market-wide stress. 
The exercise reinforced the importance of insurers continuing to test the assumptions underpinning their recovery plans. Insurers should understand where material concentrations and dependencies arise, distinguish clearly between legally enforceable arrangements and discretionary support, and assess whether that support would remain available, timely and sufficient under a market-wide stress, when groups and counterparties may face competing demands. 
Gareth Truran, Executive Director of Insurance Supervision, said:
“DyGIST was a valuable exercise to test how general insurers would respond under pressure to a combination of severe events over a three-week period. It helped shed light on firms' decision-making, the key assumptions underpinning their planned recovery actions, and the important role played by effective reinsurance arrangements. 
"The results demonstrated the financial resilience of the sector in the scenario. But as importantly, it helped insurers identify opportunities to improve how they would respond in a real market-wide stress. This should help reinforce insurers' operational preparedness for future events and continue to support policyholders and the wider economy. We are grateful to everyone who participated in the exercise.”
The PRA will use the findings to inform its ongoing supervisory approach, including its work with insurers on the governance and executability of management actions and the resilience of key dependencies. 
Notes to editors
Read the report.
A list of participating firms are included in Annex A of the following statement: Update on the 2026 Dynamic General Insurance Stress Test (DyGIST) | Bank of England – the UK's central bank
DyGIST was designed primarily to support learning and improve understanding of sector-wide responses. It was not a pass-or-fail exercise.
The results relate to the specific risks and circumstances tested in May 2026 and should not be interpreted as a comprehensive assessment of the sector’s capital position or its resilience in all circumstances.

www.bls.gov/cpi/additional-resources/series-title-changes.htm

Technical Note
Brief Explanation of the CPI
The Consumer Price Index (CPI) measures the change in prices paid by consumers for goods and services. The CPI reflects
spending patterns for each of two population groups: all urban consumers and urban wage earners and clerical workers.
The all urban consumer group represents over 90 percent of the total U.S. population. It is based on the expenditures
of almost all residents of urban or metropolitan areas, including professionals, the self-employed, the poor, the
unemployed, and retired people, as well as urban wage earners and clerical workers. Not included in the CPI are the
spending patterns of people living in rural nonmetropolitan areas, farming families, people in the Armed Forces, and
those in institutions, such as prisons and mental hospitals. Consumer inflation for all urban consumers is measured by
two indexes, namely, the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) and the Chained Consumer Price Index for
All Urban Consumers (C-CPI-U). 
The Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W) is based on the expenditures of households
included in the CPI-U definition that meet two requirements: more than one-half of the household's income must come
from clerical or wage occupations, and at least one of the household's earners must have been employed for at least 37
weeks during the previous 12 months. The CPI-W population represents approximately 30 percent of the total U.S.
population and is a subset of the CPI-U population.
The CPIs are based on prices of food, clothing, shelter, fuels, transportation, doctors' and dentists' services, drugs,
and other goods and services that people buy for day-to-day living. Prices are collected each month in 75 urban areas
across the country from about 6,000 housing units and approximately 22,000 retail establishments (department stores,
supermarkets, hospitals, and other types of stores and service establishments). All taxes directly associated with the
purchase and use of items are included in the index. Prices of fuels and a few other items are obtained every month in
all 75 locations. Prices of most other commodities and services are collected every month in the three largest
geographic areas and every other month in other areas. Prices of most goods and services are obtained by personal
visit, telephone call, web, or app collection by the Bureau's trained representatives.
In calculating the index, price changes for the various items in each location are aggregated using weights, which
represent their importance in the spending of the appropriate population group. Local data are then combined to obtain
a U.S. city average. For the CPI-U and CPI-W, separate indexes are also published by size of city, by region of the
country, for cross-classifications of regions and population-size classes, and for 23 selected local areas. Area
indexes do not measure differences in the level of prices among cities; they only measure the average change in prices
for each area since the base period. For the C-CPI-U, data are issued only at the national level. The CPI-U and CPI-W
are considered final when released, but the C-CPI-U is issued in preliminary form and subject to three subsequent
quarterly revisions.

 THE EMPLOYMENT SITUATION - OCTOBER 2026 
Total nonfarm payroll employment rose by 165,000 in October, and the unemployment rate changed 
little at 4.1 percent, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. Employment increased in 
professional and business services, in health care, and in transportation and warehousing. 
This news release presents statistics from two monthly surveys. The household survey measures labor 
force status, including unemployment, by demographic characteristics. The establishment survey 
measures nonfarm employment, hours, and earnings by industry. For more information about the 
concepts and statistical methodology used in these two surveys, see the Technical Note. 
Household Survey Data 
Both the unemployment rate, at 4.1 percent, and the number of unemployed people, at 7.1 million, 
changed little in October. The unemployment rate has remained in a narrow range of 4.1 percent to 
4.3 percent since March. (See table A-1.) 
Among the major worker groups, the unemployment rates showed little or no change in October for 
adult men (3.9 percent), adult women (3.6 percent), teenagers (13.9 percent), and people who are 
White (3.7 percent), Black (6.6 percent), Asian (2.8 percent), or Hispanic (4.7 percent). (See 
tables A-1, A-2, and A-3.) 
The number of long-term unemployed (those jobless for 27 weeks or more), at 2.0 million, changed 
little over the month. The long-term unemployed accounted for 27.6 percent of all unemployed 
people. (See table A-12.) 
Both the labor force participation rate, at 61.9 percent, and the employment-population ratio, at 
59.3 percent, changed little in October. These measures have shown little net change since January. 
(See table A-1.) 
The number of people employed part time for economic reasons increased by 339,000 to 4.8 million in 
October. These individuals would have preferred full-time employment but were working part time 
because their hours had been reduced or they were unable to find full-time jobs. (See table A-8.) 
In October, the number of people not in the labor force who currently want a job changed little at 
6.0 million. These individuals were not counted as unemployed because they were not actively 
looking for work during the 4 weeks preceding the survey or were unavailable to take a job. (See 
table A-1.) 
Among those not in the labor force who wanted a job, the number of people marginally attached to 
the labor force changed little at 1.6 million in October. These individuals wanted and were 
available for work and had looked for a job sometime in the prior 12 months but had not looked for 
work in the 4 weeks preceding the survey. The number of discouraged workers, a subset of the 
marginally attached who believed that no jobs were available for them, also changed little over 
the month at 448,000. (See Summary table A.) 
Establishment Survey Data 
Total nonfarm payroll employment rose by 165,000 in October, higher than the average monthly gain 
of 48,000 over the prior 12 months. In October, employment increased in professional and business 
services, in health care, and in transportation and warehousing. (See table B-1.) 
Employment in professional and business services increased by 70,000 in October, well above the 
average monthly gain of 15,000 over the prior 12 months. In October, employment continued to trend 
up in professional, scientific, and technical services (+33,000), in administrative and support and 
waste management and remediation services (+28,000), and in management of companies and enterprises 
(+9,000). Professional and business services has added 269,000 jobs since a recent low in October 
2025. 
Health care added 42,000 jobs in October, higher than the average monthly gain of 31,000 over the 
prior 12 months. In October, employment gains occurred in hospitals (+16,000), home health care 
services (+11,000), and outpatient care centers (+5,000). 
In October, transportation and warehousing added 25,000 jobs, reflecting growth in couriers and 
messengers (+17,000) and air transportation (+4,000). Transportation and warehousing has added 
104,000 jobs since a recent employment low in February, with couriers and messengers (+71,000) 
contributing most of the gain. 
Manufacturing employment continued to trend up in October (+19,000) and has increased by 101,000 
since a recent low in December 2025. In October, job gains occurred in computer and electronic 
product manufacturing (+7,000), machinery manufacturing (+4,000), and primary metal manufacturing 
(+4,000). 
Employment showed little change over the month in other major industries, including mining, 
quarrying, and oil and gas extraction; construction; wholesale trade; retail trade; information; 
financial activities; social assistance; leisure and hospitality; other services; and government. 
In October, average hourly earnings for all employees on private nonfarm payrolls increased by 14 
cents, or 0.4 percent, to $38.00. Over the past 12 months, average hourly earnings have increased 
by 3.1 percent. In October, average hourly earnings of private-sector production and nonsupervisory 
employees rose by 12 cents, or 0.4 percent, to $32.75. (See tables B-3 and B-8.) 
The average workweek for all employees on private nonfarm payrolls remained at 34.4 hours in 
October. In manufacturing, the average workweek was unchanged at 40.5 hours, and overtime edged up 
by 0.1 hour to 3.1 hours. The average workweek for production and nonsupervisory employees on 
private nonfarm payrolls declined by 0.1 hour to 33.8 hours. (See tables B-2 and B-7.) 
The change in total nonfarm payroll employment for August was revised up by 53,000, from +133,000 
to +186,000, and the change for September was revised up by 31,000, from +29,000 to +60,000. With 
these revisions, employment in August and September combined is 84,000 higher than previously 
reported. (Monthly revisions result from additional reports received from businesses and government 
agencies since the last published estimates and from the recalculation of seasonal factors.)

2026, at 8:30 a.m. (ET).

 PRODUCER PRICE INDEXES - OCTOBER 2026
The Producer Price Index for final demand rose 0.3 percent in October, seasonally adjusted, the 
U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. Final demand prices advanced 1.4 percent in 
September and 0.4 percent in August. (See table A.) On an unadjusted basis, the index for final 
demand increased 6.5 percent for the 12 months ended in October, the largest 12-month rise 
since moving up 7.4 percent in November 2022.
Leading the October advance in final demand prices, the index for final demand goods increased 
0.5 percent. Prices for final demand services moved up 0.2 percent.
The index for final demand less foods, energy, and trade services rose 0.5 percent in October, the 
same as in September. For the 12 months ended in October, prices for final demand less foods, 
energy, and trade services advanced 4.9 percent.
Final Demand
Final demand goods: The index for final demand goods increased 0.5 percent in October following 
a 2.5-percent rise in September. Over 60 percent of the advance in October is attributable to prices 
for final demand goods less foods and energy, which moved up 0.5 percent. The index for final 
demand foods increased 1.3 percent. In contrast, prices for final demand energy edged down 0.1 
percent. For the 12 months ended in October, the index for final demand goods increased 10.2 
percent, the largest 12-month rise since advancing 10.5 percent in October 2022.
Product detail: Within the index for final demand goods in October, prices for basic organic 
chemicals advanced 3.9 percent. The indexes for fresh and dry vegetables; gas fuels; aeronautical, 
nautical, and navigational instruments; jet fuel; and processed young chickens also moved higher. 
(See table 2.) Conversely, diesel fuel prices fell 7.9 percent. The indexes for pork and for passenger 
cars also declined. 
Final demand services: The index for final demand services moved up 0.2 percent in October, the 
fifth consecutive advance. Three-fourths of the October rise can be traced to a 2.0-percent increase in 
prices for final demand transportation and warehousing services. The index for final demand services 
less trade, transportation, and warehousing advanced 0.2 percent. In contrast, margins for final 
demand trade services decreased 0.2 percent.
Product detail: Over 80 percent of the October increase in the index for final demand services is 
attributable to prices for truck transportation of freight, which rose 3.9 percent. The indexes for fuels 
and lubricants retailing; health, beauty, and optical goods retailing; food and alcohol wholesaling; 
hospital outpatient care; and traveler accommodation services also moved higher. Conversely, 
margins for machinery and vehicle wholesaling fell 4.2 percent. Prices for system software 
publishing and for airline passenger services also declined.

for unprocessed goods fell 3.1 percent, and the index for services rose 0.6 percent. (See tables B and

Processed goods for intermediate demand: Prices for processed goods for intermediate demand 
advanced 0.4 percent in October, the third consecutive rise. Leading the October increase, the index 
for processed materials less foods and energy moved up 0.9 percent. Prices for processed foods and 
feeds advanced 1.0 percent. In contrast, the index for processed energy goods declined 1.6 percent. 
For the 12 months ended in October, prices for processed goods for intermediate demand increased 
14.6 percent, the largest 12-month rise since jumping 17.2 percent in July 2022.
Product detail: More than 40 percent of the October advance in the index for processed goods for 
intermediate demand can be traced to prices for basic organic chemicals, which moved up 3.9 
percent. The indexes for jet fuel, electronic components and accessories, natural gas liquids, 
fabricated structural metal products, and prepared animal feeds also increased. Conversely, prices for 
diesel fuel fell 7.9 percent. The indexes for pork and for lumber also decreased.
Unprocessed goods for intermediate demand: Prices for unprocessed goods for intermediate 
demand fell 3.1 percent in October, the largest decline since moving down 6.6 percent in June. 
Leading the broad-based decrease in October, the index for unprocessed energy materials dropped 
7.7 percent. Prices for unprocessed nonfood materials less energy and for unprocessed foodstuffs and 
feedstuffs also fell, 0.9 percent and 0.2 percent, respectively. For the 12 months ended in October, the 
index for unprocessed goods for intermediate demand rose 16.9 percent.
Product detail: A major factor in the October decline in the index for unprocessed goods for 
intermediate demand was a 10.3-percent decrease in prices for crude petroleum. The indexes for 
corn, slaughter hogs, wheat, aluminum base scrap, and hay and hayseeds also moved down. In 
contrast, prices for raw milk advanced 8.2 percent. The indexes for natural gas and for carbon steel 
scrap also increased.

Goods (Census basis)
Data for goods on a Census basis are compiled from the documents collected by U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and reflect the movement of goods between foreign countries and the 50 states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, and U.S. Foreign Trade Zones. They include government and non-government shipments of goods and exclude shipments between the United States and its territories and possessions; transactions with U.S. military, diplomatic, and consular installations abroad; U.S. goods returned to the United States by its Armed Forces; personal and household effects of travelers; and in-transit shipments. The General Imports value reflects the total arrival of merchandise from foreign countries that immediately enters consumption channels, warehouses, or Foreign Trade Zones.

The CIF (cost, insurance, and freight) value represents the landed value of the merchandise at the first port of arrival in the United States. Exports are valued at the f.a.s. (free alongside ship) value of merchandise at the U.S. port of export, based on the transaction price including inland freight, insurance, and other charges incurred in placing the merchandise alongside the carrier at the U.S. port of exportation.

How does EIA account for small differences between energy supply and demand data? 
Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Monthly Energy Review
Note: Supply = production + imports; demand = consumption + exports; demand - supply = stock change + other 
EIA uses over 60 surveys to collect data on the U.S. energy sector’s supply and demand. In theory, supply and demand should balance. In practice, we often have small differences between our total supply and total demand figures. 
To account for the differences between U.S. total primary energy supply and demand, our Monthly Energy Review includes a stock change and other data series, a grouping of items that account for the differences between supply and demand each month. 
These accounting differences represent a very small share of energy markets. In 2025, our combined surveys accounted for about 128 quadrillion British thermal units (quads) each for U.S. energy supply and demand, and stock change and other was 0.4 quads—about 0.3% of the total. 
Stock change is the net difference between energy held in storage at the beginning and end of a month. 
The other portion of stock change and other represents the many forms of small accounting differences: 
Differences in survey respondent accounting and reporting practices 
Differences in timing between energy activity occurrences and reporting periods 
Measurement and estimation errors 
Limitations in data collection systems and survey coverage 
Energy lost during transfers or storage 
Unreported energy activities 
To document the other differences between supply and demand, besides stock change, we use various adjustments, balancing items, and losses and unaccounted for series, a standard statistical accounting practice. Rather than indicating a flaw in the underlying statistics, these series ensure that published data are consistent and transparent, while also providing a measure of the uncertainty associated with our survey data. 
Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Monthly Energy Review
For petroleum and biofuels, our adjustments series accounts for the fact that survey responses may not precisely reflect actual activity. We’ve made improvements to our petroleum data over time to account for changes in transfers to crude oil supply, motor gasoline blending components, distillate fuel oil by pipeline operations, and other developments in petroleum markets. See Appendix B of our Petroleum Supply Monthly for more details. 
For natural gas, our balancing item series accounts for differences between supply and demand. Some of the differences are because of natural gas lost to the atmosphere. Also, there can be differences in conversions of flow data metered at varying temperatures and pressures, variations in company accounting and billing practices, and differences between billing cycles and calendar periods. See Appendix A of our Natural Gas Monthly for more details. 
For coal, we use a losses and unaccounted for series to represent differences in supply and demand, including coal lost during transport and various accounting and timing issues. In 2009, because of incomplete data coverage and different source data, biofuels have a small balancing item to balance biodiesel supply and demand.

EMBARGOED UNTIL RELEASE AT 8:30 a.m. EST, Friday, November 20, 2026
 BEA 26–49
Activities of U.S. Multinational Enterprises, 2024
Worldwide employment by U.S. multinational enterprises increased 0.9 percent to 44.2 million workers in 2024 (preliminary) from 43.8 million workers in 2023 (revised), according to statistics released today by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis on the operations and finances of U.S. parent companies and their majority-owned foreign affiliates.
Employment in the United States by U.S. parents increased 0.1 percent to 29.9 million workers in 2024. U.S. parents accounted for 67.6 percent of worldwide employment by U.S. multinational enterprises (MNEs), down from 68.1 percent in 2023. Employment abroad by foreign affiliates of U.S. MNEs increased 2.7 percent to 14.3 million workers and accounted for 32.4 percent of employment by U.S. MNEs worldwide.
U.S. parents accounted for 21.7 percent of total private industry employment in the United States in 2024, down from 21.9 percent in 2023. Employment by U.S. parents was largest in manufacturing, in “other industries,” led by transportation and warehousing, and in retail trade. Employment abroad by foreign affiliates was largest in India, Mexico, and the United Kingdom.
Worldwide current-dollar value added of U.S. MNEs increased 8.0 percent to $7.4 trillion in 2024. Value added by U.S. parents, a measure of U.S. parents’ direct contribution to U.S. gross domestic product, increased 8.5 percent to $5.7 trillion. U.S parents accounted for 21.8 percent of total U.S. private-industry value added, up from 21.2 percent in 2023. Foreign affiliate value added increased 6.5 percent to $1.8 trillion. Value added by foreign affiliates was largest in the United Kingdom, Ireland, and Canada.
Worldwide expenditures for property, plant, and equipment of U.S. MNEs increased 7.1 percent to $1.2 trillion. Expenditures by U.S. parents accounted for $968.7 billion, representing 36.5 percent of all U.S. private-business capital expenditures. Expenditures by foreign affiliates accounted for $216.2 billion.
Worldwide research and development (R&D) expenditures of U.S. MNEs increased 10.1 percent to $622.7 billion. U.S. parents accounted for expenditures of $536.5 billion, representing 69.6 percent of business R&D performed in the United States. Foreign affiliates accounted for expenditures of $86.2 billion.
Additional statistics on the activities of U.S. parent companies and their foreign affiliates, including sales, balance sheet and income statement items, compensation of employees, trade in goods, and more are available on BEA’s website. More industry detail for U.S. parents and more industry and country detail for foreign affiliates are also available on the website.
Updates to the statistics
Statistics for 2023 were revised to incorporate newly available and revised source data. Preliminary statistics for 2023 were released in August 2025.

EMBARGOED UNTIL RELEASE AT 10:00 a.m. EST, Wednesday, November 18, 2026
 BEA 26–48
Outdoor Recreation Economic Statistics, U.S. and States, 2025
New Statistics for 2025; Updates for 2021–2024
Today, the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis released new statistics measuring the outdoor recreation economy for the nation, all 50 states, and the District of Columbia. The new data show that the value added of the outdoor recreation economy accounted for 2.3 percent ($704.2 billion) of current-dollar gross domestic product (GDP) for the nation in 2025 (national table 2). Across states and the District of Columbia, value added for outdoor recreation as a share of state GDP ranged from 6.1 percent in Hawaii to 1.0 percent in the District of Columbia (state table 1).
Inflation-adjusted (“real”) GDP for the outdoor recreation economy increased 1.9 percent in 2025, compared with an increase of 2.3 percent for the overall U.S. economy, reflecting a deceleration from the 2.5 percent increase in 2024 (national table 1). In 2025, real gross output for the outdoor recreation economy increased 2.1 percent, compensation increased 4.6 percent, and employment increased 1.7 percent (national table 9).
Outdoor recreation employment increased in 43 states and the District of Columbia in 2025. The change in outdoor recreation employment ranged from 5.0 percent in Rhode Island, Kansas, and the District of Columbia to −1.1 percent in New Jersey and Alabama (BEA interactive tables).
Outdoor recreation by activity
Outdoor recreation activities fall into three general categories: (1) conventional activities such as bicycling, boating, hiking, and hunting; (2) other activities such as gardening and outdoor concerts; and (3) supporting activities such as construction, travel and tourism, local trips, and government expenditures. 
In 2025, conventional outdoor recreation accounted for 29.2 percent of U.S. outdoor recreation value added, compared with 29.1 percent in 2024. “Other outdoor recreation” accounted for 19.3 percent of value added in 2025, compared with 19.1 percent in 2024. Supporting outdoor recreation accounted for 51.5 percent of value added in 2025, compared with 51.7 percent in 2024.
Additional highlights for value added by activity for 2025 include (state table 2):
Boating/fishing was the largest conventional activity for the nation at $39.1 billion in current-dollar value added and was the largest conventional activity in 35 states and the District of Columbia. The states with the largest contributions were Florida ($4.5 billion), California ($3.3 billion), and Texas ($3.0 billion).
RVing was the second-largest conventional activity for the nation at $26.8 billion in current-dollar value added and was the largest conventional activity in 10 states. The states with the largest contributions were Indiana ($4.7 billion), Texas ($2.6 billion), and California ($2.1 billion).
Hunting/shooting/trapping was the third-largest conventional activity for the nation at $15.1 billion in current-dollar value added and was the largest conventional activity in Arizona and Wyoming. The states with the largest contributions were Texas ($1.8 billion), California ($849.8 million), and Florida ($831.3 million).
Snow activities for the nation totaled $7.8 billion in current-dollar value added and was the largest conventional activity in Colorado, Utah, and Vermont. The states with the largest contributions were Colorado ($1.8 billion), California ($735.7 million), and Utah ($640.1 million).
Outdoor recreation by industry
The outdoor recreation by industry data show the contributions of industries to the outdoor recreation economy, including their impact on value added, gross output, employment, and compensation.
For the nation, the arts, entertainment, recreation, accommodation, and food services industry group was the largest contributor to U.S. outdoor recreation in 2025, accounting for $179.5 billion, or 25.5 percent of current-dollar value added. At the state level, arts, entertainment, recreation, accommodation, and food services was the largest contributor to outdoor recreation value added in 25 states and the District of Columbia. The states with the largest contributions were California ($23.5 billion), Florida ($23.4 billion), and New York ($11.6 billion) (state table 3).
Retail trade was the second-largest industry group for the nation, at $166.5 billion, or 23.6 percent of value added, and was the largest industry group in 22 states. The states with the largest contributions were California ($19.5 billion), Texas ($14.6 billion), and Florida ($13.3 billion).
Transportation and warehousing was the third-largest industry group for the nation, at $86.4 billion, or 12.3 percent of value added, and was the largest industry group in Alaska. The states with the largest contributions were Florida ($12.8 billion), California ($10.8 billion), and Texas ($7.1 billion).
Annual update of outdoor recreation economic statistics
Estimates for 2021 to 2024 were updated to incorporate newly available and revised source data. At the national level, gross output, value added, employment, and compensation reflect the results of the 2026 annual update of the National Economic Accounts, which include the National Income and Product Accounts and the Industry Economic Accounts. The state statistics now reflect these updated national data as well as the 2026 annual update of the Regional Economic Accounts and newly available and revised regional source data.
Previously published estimates are available in BEA’s Data Archive.

 November 18, 2026 
U.S. natural gas inventories end injection season above normal levels 
Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Weekly Natural Gas Storage Report and Natural Gas Monthly 
Note: Five-year average=2021–2025 
Working natural gas in storage in the Lower 48 states ended the natural gas injection season at 3,810 billion cubic feet (Bcf), exceeding the five-year average by almost 2%, according to estimates based on data from our Weekly Natural Gas Storage Report released on November 12. Injection season runs April 1–October 31, the months of typically lower natural gas demand. 
While net injections were 2 Bcf less than the five-year average this injection season, working gas stocks are higher than usual because they started the 2026 season 3% (63 Bcf) above the five-year average at 1,878 Bcf. 
Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Weekly Natural Gas Storage Report 
Higher than average inventories at the start of the summer injection season allowed storage operators to reach their end-of-season targets with smaller incremental natural gas injections. Although total dry natural gas production during the 2026 refill season was 3% higher than the same period in 2025, according to S&P Global Energy, most of the increased production during this period was used to meet rising demand from liquefied natural gas export terminals. 
Mild spring temperatures during the first several weeks of the refill season mitigated seasonal residential and commercial natural gas demand, allowing the surplus to the five-year average to grow, peaking at 198 Bcf (7%) for the week ending August 7, before declining for the next 10 consecutive weeks, as warmer-than-normal temperatures during the summer months increased power generation demand for natural gas. Mild temperatures returned during the final weeks of the injection season, which led to above-normal injections. Weekly injections ranged from 108 Bcf in early June to 15 Bcf in late August. 
In our November Short-Term Energy Outlook, we forecast natural gas withdrawals during the 2026–2027 heating season (November 1–March 31) will total 1,900 Bcf and that inventories will be 4% above the five-year (2022–2026) average at the end of March 2027 because of a relatively mild winter and increases in natural gas production.
